problems.name: Two Sum
problems.description: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return the indices of two numbers that add up to target. You may assume that each input has exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice. Return the indices in any order.
edge_cases: Minimum length (2 elements) that sum to target.
Duplicate numbers (e.g., [3,3] target 6) - must return indices 0 and 1.

hidden_test_cases.reason: Multiple valid pairs, ensure correct indices.

hints: Think about whether you can avoid checking every pair.
A hash-based data structure can help you remember values you've already seen.
For each number, check whether target - number has already appeared.

solution_approach.key_observation: For each element, we only need to know if the complement exists among previously seen numbers.
solution_approach.algorithm: Iterate through the array, maintaining a hash map of numbers to their indices. For each num, compute complement = target - num. If complement is in the map, return its index and current index. Otherwise, store num with its index.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We guarantee finding the pair because we check complements before inserting the current element, ensuring we don't use the same element twice.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use a Map<int, int> for storing value to index. Ensure to check existence before adding current.

problems.what_you_learn: How to use a hash map to reduce pair searching from quadratic to linear time.
common_mistakes: Using brute force O(n^2) when an O(n) solution is expected.
Using the same element twice (e.g., checking complement == num before adding current).

problems.name: Valid Anagram
problems.description: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, and false otherwise. An anagram is a word formed by rearranging the letters of another word.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: The two strings have the same letter counts.

edge_cases: Strings of equal length but different characters.
Strings of different length (cannot be anagrams).

hidden_test_cases.reason: Check if all letters are accounted.

hints: Compare the frequency of each character in both strings.
Use a hash map to count characters from one string, then decrement while iterating through the other.
Alternatively, sort both strings and compare.

solution_approach.key_observation: Anagram strings have identical character counts.
solution_approach.algorithm: If lengths differ, return false. Use a dictionary to count frequencies of characters in s. Then iterate through t and decrement counts; if any count goes negative or a character is missing, return false. Finally, return true.
solution_approach.why_it_works: The counts must match exactly; decrementing validates that t uses exactly the same letters.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use a Map or a 26-element array for lowercase letters. For Unicode, use Map.

common_mistakes: Using sorting which is O(n log n) and may not be optimal.

problems.name: Contains Duplicate
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice in the array, and false if every element is distinct.
hints: Think about how you can remember which numbers you've already seen.
A hash set can store elements in O(1) average time.
If you encounter an element already in the set, return true.

solution_approach.key_observation: We need to detect any duplicate in a single pass.
solution_approach.algorithm: Iterate through the array, inserting each element into a hash set. If an element is already present, return true. After loop, return false.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Any duplicate will be detected when we attempt to add it for the second time.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use a HashSet<int> for O(1) average lookups.

problems.what_you_learn: Using hash set for duplicate detection.
common_mistakes: Using a brute force O(n^2) approach.
Returning true when array is empty (though constraints say min length 1).

problems.name: Missing Number
problems.description: Given an array nums containing n distinct numbers taken from the range [0, n], return the only number in that range that is missing from the array.
edge_cases: All numbers present except one at boundary.
hints: The sum of numbers from 0 to n is n*(n+1)/2. Subtract the sum of the array to find the missing number.
Alternatively, use XOR: x ^ x = 0, so XOR all numbers from 0 to n and all array elements to cancel out.
Both methods give O(n) time and O(1) space.

solution_approach.key_observation: The sum of the range minus the actual sum gives the missing number.
solution_approach.algorithm: Compute total = n*(n+1)//2. Subtract sum(nums) to get missing.
solution_approach.why_it_works: The total sum includes all numbers; the difference is the missing one.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Watch for integer overflow; in Dart, use BigInt if needed, but constraints are within safe range.

problems.what_you_learn: Using sum formula or XOR to find missing element.
common_mistakes: Using sorting which is O(n log n).

problems.name: Single Number
problems.description: Given a non-empty array of integers nums, every element appears twice except for one. Find that single one. Implement a solution with linear runtime complexity and use only constant extra space.
constraints: Each element appears twice except for one.
hints: Use the XOR bitwise operator: a ^ a = 0, a ^ 0 = a.
XOR all numbers together; pairs will cancel out, leaving the single number.
This uses constant extra space.

solution_approach.key_observation: XOR is commutative and associative, and pairs cancel.
solution_approach.algorithm: Initialize result = 0. For each num in nums, result ^= num. Return result.
solution_approach.why_it_works: All numbers that appear twice will cancel to 0; the remaining number is the answer.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Ensure to use XOR operator (^).

problems.what_you_learn: Bitwise XOR for finding unique elements.
common_mistakes: Using sorting or hash map, which uses extra space.
Not handling negative numbers correctly (XOR works fine).

problems.name: Move Zeroes
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, move all 0's to the end of it while maintaining the relative order of the non-zero elements. Do this in-place without making a copy of the array.
hints: Use two pointers: one to keep track of the position to place the next non-zero element.
Iterate through the array, and whenever you encounter a non-zero, swap it with the element at the write pointer.
This maintains order and moves zeros to the end.

solution_approach.key_observation: We can treat the array as a sequence where we overwrite zeros with non-zeros.
solution_approach.algorithm: Maintain an index 'write' starting at 0. Iterate 'i' from 0 to n-1. If nums[i] != 0, assign nums[write] = nums[i] and increment write. After loop, fill the remaining positions from write to end with zeros.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We compact non-zero elements to the front, preserving order, then fill rest with zeros.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: This is O(n) time and O(1) space. Swap version is also possible.

problems.what_you_learn: In-place array manipulation using two pointers.
follow_up_concepts: Partitioning arrays (e.g., partition based on condition).
common_mistakes: Creating a new array (violates in-place requirement).
Not preserving relative order of non-zeros.

problems.name: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
problems.description: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the i-th day. You want to maximize your profit by choosing a single day to buy one stock and a different day in the future to sell it. Return the maximum profit you can achieve. If no profit is possible, return 0.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 2 (price=1) and sell on day 5 (price=6), profit=5.

hints: You can only buy before you sell, so you need to track the minimum price seen so far.
For each day, compute potential profit if you sell on that day using the minimum price so far.
Keep track of the maximum profit.

solution_approach.key_observation: Maximum profit can be found by maintaining the minimum price and computing difference for each day.
solution_approach.algorithm: Initialize minPrice = infinity, maxProfit = 0. Iterate prices: if current price < minPrice, update minPrice; else, compute profit = current - minPrice and update maxProfit if larger.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We simulate buying at the lowest price before selling, ensuring we sell after buying.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: This is a classic greedy/DP one-pass solution.

problems.what_you_learn: Single pass optimization for array problems.
follow_up_concepts: Multiple transactions (Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II)

problems.name: Merge Sorted Array
problems.description: You are given two integer arrays nums1 and nums2, sorted in non-decreasing order, and two integers m and n representing the number of elements in nums1 and nums2 respectively. Merge nums2 into nums1 as one sorted array. The final sorted array should be stored inside nums1 (which has length m+n).

function_signature.generic: merge(nums1: List[int], m: int, nums2: List[int], n: int) -> None
function_signature.dart: void merge(List<int> nums1, int m, List<int> nums2, int n)

edge_cases: All elements in nums2 smaller than nums1.
All elements in nums2 larger than nums1.
hints: Merge from the end to avoid overwriting elements in nums1.
Use three pointers: i = m-1 (last element of nums1's actual elements), j = n-1 (last of nums2), k = m+n-1 (last position in nums1).
Compare nums1[i] and nums2[j] and place the larger at nums1[k], then decrement pointers.

solution_approach.key_observation: Merging from the back allows us to avoid extra space.
solution_approach.algorithm: Set i = m-1, j = n-1, k = m+n-1. While i >= 0 and j >= 0: if nums1[i] > nums2[j] then nums1[k--] = nums1[i--] else nums1[k--] = nums2[j--]. After loop, if j >= 0, copy remaining nums2 into nums1.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We place elements in correct final positions, avoiding overwriting needed elements.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Ensure to handle cases where one array is exhausted.

problems.what_you_learn: In-place merging of two sorted arrays from the end.
common_mistakes: Starting from the front, overwriting elements.
Not handling case where i < 0 but j >= 0.

problems.name: Plus One
problems.description: You are given a large integer represented as an integer array digits, where each digits[i] is the i-th digit of the integer. The digits are ordered from most significant to least significant. Increment the integer by one and return the resulting array.
constraints: No leading zeros except for the number 0 itself.

hidden_test_cases.reason: Large length with no carry except last.

hints: Start from the least significant digit (rightmost) and add 1.
If a digit becomes 10, set it to 0 and carry over to the next digit.
If you carry past the most significant digit, prepend a 1 to the array.

solution_approach.key_observation: The only time we need to expand the array is when all digits are 9.
solution_approach.algorithm: Iterate from the end; add 1 to the last digit. If it becomes 10, set to 0 and continue to previous. If we finish loop without returning, it means all digits were 9, so create a new array of length+1 with first element 1 and rest zeros.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Simulates addition of one exactly.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use a for loop from i = n-1 down to 0. If digits[i] < 9, increment and return; else set to 0. After loop, prepend 1.

problems.expected_space_complexity: O(1) or O(n) for overflow case
problems.what_you_learn: Simulating arithmetic operations on array representations.
follow_up_concepts: Add two numbers represented as arrays
common_mistakes: Returning an array with leading zero.

problems.name: Valid Palindrome
problems.description: A phrase is a palindrome if, after converting all uppercase letters to lowercase and removing all non-alphanumeric characters, it reads the same forward and backward. Given a string s, return true if it is a palindrome, otherwise false.
constraints: s consists of printable ASCII characters.

input.s: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

examples.explanation: After cleaning: 'raceacar' which is not palindrome.

input.s: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

hints: Clean the string first: remove non-alphanumeric and convert to lower case.
Then use two pointers: one at start, one at end, compare characters.
If any mismatch, return false.

solution_approach.key_observation: We only need to compare alphanumeric characters ignoring case.
solution_approach.algorithm: Initialize two pointers i=0, j=s.length-1. While i < j: skip non-alphanumeric characters on both ends; compare lowercased characters; if mismatch return false; else move pointers.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We directly compare characters in the original string without building a new one.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use Character.isLetterOrDigit (Dart: String.codeUnitAt, etc.).

problems.what_you_learn: Two-pointer technique for palindrome verification with skipping.
common_mistakes: Creating a new cleaned string (extra space).

problems.name: Reverse String
problems.description: Write a function that reverses a string. The input string is given as an array of characters s. You must do this by modifying the input array in-place with O(1) extra memory.
constraints: s consists of printable ASCII characters.
hints: Use two pointers: one at the beginning, one at the end.
Swap the characters at the two pointers and move them towards each other.
Stop when the pointers cross.

solution_approach.key_observation: Reversing in-place can be done by swapping pairs.
solution_approach.algorithm: Set left = 0, right = s.length - 1. While left < right: swap s[left] and s[right]; left++; right--;
solution_approach.why_it_works: Each swap correctly places characters in reverse order.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use a temporary variable or destructuring for swap.

problems.what_you_learn: In-place array reversal using two pointers.
common_mistakes: Not handling Unicode properly (but constraints assume ASCII).

problems.name: First Unique Character in a String
problems.description: Given a string s, find the first non-repeating character and return its index. If it does not exist, return -1.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: The first non-repeating is 'v' at index 2.

hints: Count the frequency of each character.
Then iterate through the string again and find the first character with frequency 1.
Use a hash map or array of size 26.

solution_approach.key_observation: We need frequency count to know if a character repeats.
solution_approach.algorithm: First pass: build a frequency map (array of 26). Second pass: iterate through s and return the index of the first character with count 1.
solution_approach.why_it_works: The first character with count 1 is the first non-repeating.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use a List<int> of size 26, increment counts. Then second loop.

common_mistakes: Using a hash map that uses O(n) space, but okay.

problems.name: Find the Difference
problems.description: You are given two strings s and t. String t is generated by random shuffling string s and then adding one more letter at a random position. Return the letter that was added to t.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Use XOR on all characters of both strings; the extra character will remain.
Alternatively, compute frequency difference.
XOR is efficient and O(1) space.

solution_approach.key_observation: XOR of all characters in s and t will cancel out common characters, leaving the extra one.
solution_approach.algorithm: Initialize result = 0. XOR all characters from s and t. The result is the ASCII of the added character.
solution_approach.why_it_works: A character XORed with itself is 0; the extra character appears odd times.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use charCodeAt or code unit. Return String.fromCharCode(result).

common_mistakes: Using hash map which uses O(n) space.

problems.name: Longest Common Prefix
problems.description: Write a function to find the longest common prefix string amongst an array of strings. If there is no common prefix, return an empty string.
constraints: strs[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Start with the first string as the prefix, then iterate through others, shortening the prefix as needed.
Alternatively, compare characters column by column.
Use the prefix string and trim it by comparing with each string.

solution_approach.key_observation: The common prefix cannot be longer than any string, and we can reduce it.
solution_approach.algorithm: Take the first string as prefix. For each other string, while the string does not start with prefix, shorten prefix by removing last character. Return prefix.
solution_approach.why_it_works: The prefix is gradually refined to match all strings.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use startsWith or substring.

problems.expected_time_complexity: O(S) where S is sum of all characters
common_mistakes: Index out of bounds when prefix length exceeds string length.
Using vertical scanning might be simpler but both are fine.

problems.name: Climbing Stairs
problems.description: You are climbing a staircase. It takes n steps to reach the top. Each time you can either climb 1 or 2 steps. In how many distinct ways can you climb to the top?

hidden_test_cases.reason: Max value fits in 32-bit signed int.

hints: The number of ways to reach step i is the sum of ways to reach i-1 and i-2.
This is the Fibonacci sequence.
You can solve iteratively to avoid recursion.

solution_approach.key_observation: Ways(n) = Ways(n-1) + Ways(n-2).
solution_approach.algorithm: Use iteration: if n <= 2 return n. Set a=1, b=2. For i=3..n: c = a+b; a=b; b=c. Return b.
solution_approach.why_it_works: This builds the Fibonacci sequence efficiently.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Avoid recursion due to stack and repeated work.

problems.name: Power of Two
problems.description: Given an integer n, return true if it is a power of two. Otherwise, return false. An integer n is a power of two if there exists an integer x such that n == 2^x.
hints: A power of two has exactly one bit set in binary.
Use n & (n-1) trick: for power of two, n & (n-1) == 0.
Also check n > 0.

solution_approach.key_observation: Powers of two have binary representation with a single 1.
solution_approach.algorithm: Return n > 0 and (n & (n-1)) == 0.
solution_approach.why_it_works: n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit; if it was the only bit, result is 0.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Handle n=0 separately.

problems.what_you_learn: Bit manipulation trick to check power of two.
common_mistakes: Using float log which can have precision issues.

problems.name: Number of 1 Bits
problems.description: Write a function that takes an unsigned integer and returns the number of '1' bits it has (also known as the Hamming weight).
constraints: The input is a 32-bit unsigned integer.
hints: Iterate through each bit and count.
Use n & (n-1) to clear the lowest set bit and count how many times you can do that.
Alternatively, use built-in bitCount or loop 32 times.

solution_approach.key_observation: Each iteration of n & (n-1) removes one set bit.
solution_approach.algorithm: Set count = 0. While n != 0: n = n & (n-1); count++. Return count.
solution_approach.why_it_works: The operation clears the least significant 1 bit, counting total ones.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Works for non-negative integers; Dart int is arbitrary precision, but we assume 32-bit.

common_mistakes: Using built-in functions when asked to implement.
Not handling large numbers correctly (but constraints limit to 32-bit).
Infinite loop if n is negative (but input is unsigned).

problems.name: Reverse Linked List
problems.description: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list, and return the new head.
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is in range [0, 5000].
hints: Iteratively, maintain previous, current, and next pointers.
Change the next pointer of current to previous, then move all pointers forward.
Recursively, reverse the rest of the list and then adjust the head.

solution_approach.key_observation: Each node's next should point to its previous node.
solution_approach.algorithm: Iterative: prev = null, curr = head. While curr != null: nextTemp = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = nextTemp. Return prev.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We reverse links one by one.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Be careful to save next before overwriting.

problems.what_you_learn: In-place reversal of singly linked list.
follow_up_concepts: Reverse a linked list in groups
common_mistakes: Using recursion that may stack overflow for large list (but iterative is better).

problems.name: Middle of the Linked List
problems.description: Given the head of a singly linked list, return the middle node of the linked list. If there are two middle nodes, return the second middle node.
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is in range [1, 100].
hints: Use two pointers: slow moves one step, fast moves two steps.
When fast reaches the end, slow will be at the middle.
Return slow.

solution_approach.key_observation: Moving fast twice as fast as slow ensures slow is at the middle.
solution_approach.algorithm: Set slow = head, fast = head. While fast != null and fast.next != null: slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next. Return slow.
solution_approach.why_it_works: By the time fast reaches end, slow has moved half the distance.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Check null safety for fast.next.

problems.what_you_learn: Fast and slow pointer technique for finding middle.
common_mistakes: Not handling even length correctly (should return second middle).

problems.name: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problems.description: You are given the heads of two sorted linked lists list1 and list2. Merge the two lists into one sorted list. The list should be made by splicing together the nodes of the first two lists. Return the head of the merged linked list.
constraints: The number of nodes in both lists is in range [0, 50].
Both lists are sorted in non-decreasing order.
edge_cases: All values in one list smaller than the other.
hints: Create a dummy node to simplify handling the head.
Iterate while both lists are non-empty: pick the smaller value and advance.
Append the remaining nodes of the non-empty list.

solution_approach.key_observation: We can merge by comparing heads.
solution_approach.algorithm: Create a dummy node. Maintain current pointer. While both not null: if list1.val <= list2.val, attach list1 node and move list1, else attach list2. After loop, attach the rest of non-null list. Return dummy.next.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We always pick the smallest available node.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Be careful to advance pointers.

common_mistakes: Not using a dummy node, making head insertion messy.
Infinite loop if not advancing pointers.

problems.name: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
problems.description: Given a sorted array nums, remove the duplicates in-place such that each element appears only once and return the new length. Do not allocate extra space; modify the input array in-place with O(1) extra memory.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order.

examples.explanation: New length is 2, first two elements are 1 and 2.
New length is 5, first five elements are 0,1,2,3,4.

hints: Since the array is sorted, duplicates are adjacent.
Use two pointers: one to iterate (i) and one to place unique elements (write).
Whenever nums[i] != nums[i-1], place it at write and increment.

solution_approach.key_observation: Duplicates are consecutive in sorted array.
solution_approach.algorithm: If nums.length == 0, return 0. Set write = 1. For i from 1 to n-1: if nums[i] != nums[i-1], then nums[write] = nums[i]; write++. Return write.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We copy unique elements to the front.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: The array's first write elements are the unique ones.

problems.what_you_learn: In-place duplicate removal in sorted array.
follow_up_concepts: Remove duplicates II (allow at most two)

problems.name: Remove Element
problems.description: Given an array nums and a value val, remove all occurrences of val in-place and return the new length. The order of the elements may be changed. Then return the new length.
hints: Use a pointer to place non-val elements.
Iterate through array, when nums[i] != val, place it at the pointer and increment.
The pointer will be the new length.

solution_approach.key_observation: We can overwrite elements not equal to val.
solution_approach.algorithm: Set write = 0. For i in 0..n-1: if nums[i] != val, nums[write] = nums[i]; write++. Return write.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We compact the elements that should remain.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: This preserves order if desired (but order not required).

problems.what_you_learn: In-place removal of elements from array.

problems.name: Search Insert Position
problems.description: Given a sorted array of distinct integers and a target value, return the index if the target is found. If not, return the index where it would be inserted to maintain order. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.
constraints: nums is sorted in ascending order.
hints: Binary search is the required approach.
Maintain low and high pointers. Compute mid.
If nums[mid] == target, return mid. If target < nums[mid], high = mid-1, else low = mid+1. Return low after loop.

solution_approach.key_observation: Binary search can find insertion point.
solution_approach.algorithm: Set lo=0, hi=n-1. While lo <= hi: mid = (lo+hi)//2. If nums[mid] == target: return mid. Else if target < nums[mid]: hi = mid-1. Else: lo = mid+1. Return lo.
solution_approach.why_it_works: The loop narrows down to the insertion point; lo is the first index where nums[lo] > target or lo == n.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Handle empty array? constraints say length >=1, but can generalize.

problems.what_you_learn: Binary search for sorted array and insertion point.
follow_up_concepts: First and last position in sorted array
common_mistakes: Returning mid instead of low after loop.

problems.name: Binary Search
problems.description: Given an array of integers nums which is sorted in ascending order, and an integer target, write a function to search target in nums. If target exists, return its index. Otherwise, return -1. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.
constraints: All values in nums are unique.
nums is sorted in ascending order.
hints: Use two pointers, low and high, and compute mid.
If target equals nums[mid], return mid.
If target is less, search left half; else search right half.

solution_approach.key_observation: Binary search halves the search space each step.
solution_approach.algorithm: Standard binary search loop.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Because array is sorted, we can discard half each time.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Avoid integer overflow when computing mid (use lo + (hi-lo)//2).

common_mistakes: Infinite loop due to incorrect mid calculation or pointer updates.
Not using distinct values (but constraints say unique).
Forgetting to return -1 when not found.

problems.name: Sqrt(x)
problems.description: Given a non-negative integer x, return the square root of x rounded down to the nearest integer. The returned integer should be non-negative as well. You must not use any built-in exponent function or operator. For example, do not use pow(x, 0.5) or x ** 0.5.
hints: Binary search on the range [0, x] to find the largest integer whose square <= x.
Alternatively, use Newton's method.
Be careful about overflow when computing mid*mid.

solution_approach.key_observation: The square root of x lies between 0 and x.
solution_approach.algorithm: Use binary search: lo=0, hi=x. While lo <= hi: mid = lo + (hi-lo)//2. If mid*mid <= x, set ans=mid and lo=mid+1; else hi=mid-1. Return ans.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We find the largest number whose square is <= x.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use long (or BigInt) to avoid overflow in mid*mid.

problems.what_you_learn: Binary search for finding floor square root.
common_mistakes: Not handling x=0 or x=1 correctly.

problems.name: Guess Number Higher or Lower
problems.description: We are playing the Guess Game. The game is as follows: I pick a number from 1 to n. You have to guess which number I picked. Every time you guess wrong, I will tell you whether the number I picked is higher or lower than your guess. You call a pre-defined API int guess(int num) which returns 3 possible results: -1: my number is lower (i.e., pick < num), 1: my number is higher (pick > num), 0: correct. Return the number I picked.
hints: Use binary search to find the number.
Call guess(mid) and adjust lo/hi based on result.
If guess(mid) == 0, return mid.

solution_approach.key_observation: guess API provides feedback to narrow search.
solution_approach.algorithm: Set lo=1, hi=n. While lo <= hi: mid = lo + (hi-lo)//2; res = guess(mid); if res == 0 return mid; else if res == -1: hi = mid-1; else: lo = mid+1.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Standard binary search with feedback.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: The guess API is provided by the platform.

problems.name: Isomorphic Strings
problems.description: Given two strings s and t, determine if they are isomorphic. Two strings are isomorphic if the characters in s can be replaced to get t. All occurrences of a character must be replaced with another character while preserving the order of characters. No two characters may map to the same character, but a character may map to itself.
constraints: s and t consist of any valid ASCII character.

examples.explanation: o->a and o->r? Actually o maps to a and r? Not allowed.

edge_cases: Length 0? but constraints say at least 1.

hidden_test_cases.reason: b and a both map to a? Actually a->a, b->a not allowed.

hints: Create a mapping from characters in s to characters in t.
Also ensure no two different characters in s map to the same character in t.
Use two maps or one map and a set for the target characters.

solution_approach.key_observation: Mapping must be bijective (one-to-one).
solution_approach.algorithm: Use a Map<char, char> for s->t mapping, and a Set<char> for used t characters. Iterate through characters: if s char not in map, but t char already used, return false; else add mapping. If s char in map, check if map[s] == t char; else false. Return true.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Ensures consistent mapping and no conflicts.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: For ASCII, arrays of size 256 can be used for fast mapping.

problems.expected_space_complexity: O(1) if fixed alphabet, else O(n)
common_mistakes: Only checking one direction of mapping.
Not handling non-ASCII characters (but constraints allow any).
Using two maps but not checking both directions.

problems.name: Word Pattern
problems.description: Given a pattern and a string s, find if s follows the same pattern. Here follow means a full match, such that there is a bijection between a letter in pattern and a non-empty word in s.
constraints: pattern contains only lower-case English letters.
s contains only lowercase English letters and spaces ' '.
s does not contain leading or trailing spaces.
All words in s are separated by a single space.

examples.explanation: a->dog, b->cat, but last a->fish? Actually a->dog and a->fish conflict.

hints: Split s into words. If pattern length != number of words, return false.
Create a mapping from pattern character to word, and also ensure no two pattern chars map to same word.
Use two maps or a map and a set.

solution_approach.key_observation: This is similar to isomorphic strings but with words.
solution_approach.algorithm: Split s into words. If lengths differ, return false. Use Map<char, String> for pattern to word, and Set<String> for used words. Iterate, apply bijection check.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Ensures consistent mapping.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use split(' ') to get words.

common_mistakes: Not handling multiple spaces (but constraints say single).

problems.name: Ransom Note
problems.description: Given two strings ransomNote and magazine, return true if ransomNote can be constructed by using the letters from magazine and false otherwise. Each letter in magazine can only be used once in ransomNote.
constraints: ransomNote and magazine consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Count the frequency of each character in magazine.
Then iterate through ransomNote and decrement counts; if any count goes negative, return false.
Return true if all characters satisfied.

solution_approach.key_observation: We need enough occurrences of each character in magazine.
solution_approach.algorithm: Build a frequency map of magazine. For each char in ransomNote: if count[char] == 0, return false; else decrement. Return true.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We check if we have enough letters.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use array of size 26 for lowercase.

problems.name: Balanced Binary Tree
problems.description: Given a binary tree, determine if it is height-balanced. A height-balanced binary tree is defined as a binary tree in which the left and right subtrees of every node differ in height by no more than 1.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in range [0, 5000].
hints: Compute the height of each subtree and check the difference.
Use a recursive function that returns the height if balanced, else -1.
If any subtree is unbalanced, propagate -1 up.

solution_approach.key_observation: We need to check balance and compute height simultaneously.
solution_approach.algorithm: Define helper dfs(node) returning height if balanced else -1. For each node, recursively get left height, right height; if either -1 or abs(left-right)>1 return -1; else return max(left,right)+1. At root, return dfs(root) != -1.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We compute heights and check balance in one pass.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use -1 to signal unbalanced.

common_mistakes: Computing height separately for each node causing O(n^2).
Using recursion that might overflow for deep trees (but constraints moderate).

problems.name: Valid Parentheses
problems.description: Given a string s containing just the characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', determine if the input string is valid. An input string is valid if: open brackets are closed by the same type, open brackets are closed in the correct order, and every close bracket has a corresponding open bracket.
hints: Use a stack to keep track of opening brackets.
When you see a closing bracket, check if it matches the top of the stack.
At the end, the stack should be empty.

solution_approach.key_observation: The last unmatched opening bracket must match the current closing bracket.
solution_approach.algorithm: Iterate through s. If char is opening, push to stack. If closing, if stack empty or top doesn't match, return false; else pop. After loop, return stack.isEmpty.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Stack ensures correct order and matching.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use a Map for matching pairs.

common_mistakes: Not checking stack empty before popping.
Forgetting to return false if stack not empty.

problems.name: 3Sum
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, return all the triplets [nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]] such that i != j, i != k, j != k, and nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0. The solution set must not contain duplicate triplets.
hints: Sort the array first.
For each element, use two-pointer technique to find pairs that sum to -nums[i].
Skip duplicates to avoid duplicate triplets.

solution_approach.key_observation: After sorting, we can use two pointers to find pairs.
solution_approach.algorithm: Sort nums. Iterate i from 0 to n-3. Skip duplicates for i. Set left=i+1, right=n-1. While left<right: sum = nums[i]+nums[left]+nums[right]. If sum==0, add triplet, move left and right skipping duplicates. If sum<0, left++; else right--.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Two pointers efficiently find pairs for a fixed i in sorted array.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Careful with duplicate handling.

common_mistakes: Using hash map for O(n^2) but duplicate handling hard.

problems.name: Subarray Sum Equals K
problems.description: Given an array of integers nums and an integer k, return the total number of continuous subarrays whose sum equals to k.
hints: Use prefix sum and a hash map to store frequency of prefix sums.
For each prefix sum, check if (prefix_sum - k) exists in map.
Initialize map with {0:1} to account for subarrays starting from index 0.

solution_approach.key_observation: Sum of subarray i..j = prefix[j] - prefix[i-1]. So we need to find number of i such that prefix[i-1] = prefix[j] - k.
solution_approach.algorithm: Maintain a map count of prefix sums seen. For each num, update current sum. If (current - k) is in map, add its count. Then increment count of current.
solution_approach.why_it_works: The map tracks how many times a given prefix sum has occurred, allowing O(1) lookup.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use Map<int, int> for counts.

problems.what_you_learn: Prefix sum with hash map for subarray sum count.

problems.name: Maximum Subarray
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one number) which has the largest sum and return its sum.
hints: Use Kadane's algorithm: maintain current subarray sum and max sum.
At each element, decide whether to start a new subarray or extend existing one.
If current sum becomes negative, reset to 0 (but careful for all negative).

solution_approach.key_observation: The maximum subarray ending at i is either nums[i] or nums[i] + max ending at i-1.
solution_approach.algorithm: Initialize maxSum = nums[0], currSum = nums[0]. For i from 1: currSum = max(nums[i], currSum + nums[i]); maxSum = max(maxSum, currSum). Return maxSum.
solution_approach.why_it_works: This is the classic Kadane's algorithm.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Handles all negative by choosing the largest element.

problems.what_you_learn: Kadane's algorithm for maximum subarray sum.
common_mistakes: Not handling all negative correctly (return 0 instead of max).
Using divide and conquer without understanding.

problems.name: Product of Array Except Self
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is equal to the product of all the elements of nums except nums[i]. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time and without using the division operation.
constraints: The product of any prefix or suffix fits in a 32-bit integer.
hints: Compute prefix products and suffix products.
You can do it with two passes: first pass compute left products, second pass multiply by right products.
Avoid division by using multiplication.

solution_approach.key_observation: Product except self = product of left elements * product of right elements.
solution_approach.algorithm: Create answer array. First pass: answer[i] = product of all elements to left. Second pass: maintain variable right_product; for i from n-1 to 0, answer[i] *= right_product; right_product *= nums[i]. Return answer.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We compute left products in first pass, right products on the fly.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: No division used.

common_mistakes: Not using a separate array for output.

problems.name: Find All Anagrams in a String
problems.description: Given two strings s and p, return an array of all the start indices of p's anagrams in s. You may return the answer in any order.
constraints: s and p consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Use sliding window of size p.length.
Maintain a frequency map of the current window.
Compare with the frequency map of p to detect anagram.

solution_approach.key_observation: Anagram check can be done via frequency counts.
solution_approach.algorithm: Create frequency map for p. Iterate through s with window length = p.length. Maintain window frequency. If window freq equals p freq, add start index. Slide window by updating counts.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We check each contiguous window of the same length.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use array of 26 for efficiency.

common_mistakes: Using sorting for each window O(n*k log k).

problems.name: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.description: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
constraints: s consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces.
hints: Use sliding window with two pointers: left and right.
Maintain a set of characters in current window.
When a character repeats, move left pointer to remove the duplicate.

solution_approach.key_observation: We expand right and shrink left when we see a duplicate.
solution_approach.algorithm: Set left=0, maxLen=0, charSet=set(). For right in range(n): while s[right] in charSet: charSet.remove(s[left]); left++. charSet.add(s[right]); maxLen = max(maxLen, right-left+1). Return maxLen.
solution_approach.why_it_works: The window always contains unique characters.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use Set for O(1) operations.

problems.expected_space_complexity: O(min(m, n)) where m is charset size
problems.what_you_learn: Sliding window for longest substring without repeats.
common_mistakes: Not updating max after moving left.
Using a map to track last occurrence for O(n) but set works.

problems.name: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
problems.description: Given an array of positive integers nums and a positive integer target, return the minimal length of a contiguous subarray whose sum is at least target. If there is no such subarray, return 0.
hints: Use sliding window with two pointers.
Expand right to add sum, while sum >= target, update min and shrink left.
Works since all numbers are positive.

solution_approach.key_observation: Positive numbers allow two-pointer sliding window to find minimal length.
solution_approach.algorithm: Set left=0, sum=0, minLen=INF. For right in range(n): sum += nums[right]; while sum >= target: minLen = min(minLen, right-left+1); sum -= nums[left]; left++. Return minLen if != INF else 0.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We maintain window sum and shrink when condition met.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Because all positive, we can shrink safely.

problems.what_you_learn: Sliding window for minimum subarray length with positive numbers.
common_mistakes: Using binary search for O(n log n) but sliding window is better.

problems.name: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
problems.description: You are given a string s and an integer k. You can choose any character of the string and change it to any other uppercase English character. You may perform this operation at most k times. Return the length of the longest substring containing the same letter you can get after performing the operations.
constraints: s consists of uppercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Change one 'B' to 'A' or one 'A' to 'B' to get length 4.

hidden_test_cases.reason: Can change B to A or vice versa.

hints: Use sliding window and track the frequency of characters in the window.
The number of changes needed in a window is window length - max frequency.
If changes <= k, window is valid; expand right; else shrink left.

solution_approach.key_observation: The condition for a window to be valid is (right-left+1) - maxCount <= k.
solution_approach.algorithm: Sliding window: maintain counts and maxCount. Expand right; update counts, maxCount. While windowSize - maxCount > k: decrement left char, left++. Update maxLen = max(maxLen, windowSize).
solution_approach.why_it_works: We want the longest window where we can change at most k characters to make all same.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use array of size 26 for counts.

problems.what_you_learn: Sliding window with frequency tracking and max frequency.
follow_up_concepts: Longest substring with at most k distinct characters
common_mistakes: Using while loop with condition that may be expensive but it's O(n).

problems.name: Permutation in String
problems.description: Given two strings s1 and s2, return true if s2 contains a permutation of s1. In other words, one of s1's permutations is a substring of s2.
constraints: s1 and s2 consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Use sliding window of size s1.length.
Compare frequency of window with s1 frequency.
If match, return true.

solution_approach.key_observation: Permutation means same character counts.
solution_approach.algorithm: Compute frequency of s1. Slide window over s2, maintain window freq. If they match, return true. Else slide.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Any window with same freq as s1 is a permutation.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use array of 26 for efficiency.

common_mistakes: Not handling case where s1 longer than s2.

problems.name: Koko Eating Bananas
problems.description: Koko loves to eat bananas. There are n piles of bananas, the i-th pile has piles[i] bananas. The guards have gone and will come back in h hours. Koko can decide her bananas-per-hour eating speed of k. Each hour, she chooses some pile of bananas and eats k bananas from that pile. If the pile has less than k bananas, she eats all of them and won't eat any more bananas during that hour. Return the minimum integer k such that she can eat all the bananas within h hours.

examples.explanation: Need speed 30 to finish in 5 hours.

hints: The answer lies between 1 and max(piles). Use binary search.
For a given speed k, compute total hours needed: sum(ceil(pile/k)).
If total hours <= h, we can try smaller speed.

solution_approach.key_observation: Time needed is non-increasing as speed increases.
solution_approach.algorithm: Binary search low=1, high=max(piles). While low < high: mid = (low+high)//2; hours = sum((p + mid - 1)//mid for p in piles); if hours <= h: high = mid; else: low = mid+1. Return low.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Binary search on monotonic function.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use ceil division: (p + k - 1)//k.

problems.what_you_learn: Binary search on answer with feasibility check.
follow_up_concepts: Capacity to ship packages within D days

problems.name: Find Peak Element
problems.description: A peak element is an element that is strictly greater than its neighbors. Given a 0-indexed integer array nums, find a peak element, and return its index. If the array contains multiple peaks, return the index to any of the peaks. You may assume nums[-1] = nums[n] = -∞.
constraints: nums[i] != nums[i+1] for all i (no adjacent equals)
hints: Use binary search: if nums[mid] < nums[mid+1], then peak is on the right; else peak is on the left (including mid).
This works because of the alternating nature and no equal adjacent.
Return any peak.

solution_approach.key_observation: If mid is not peak, we can move to the side with a larger neighbor.
solution_approach.algorithm: Set lo=0, hi=n-1. While lo < hi: mid = (lo+hi)//2; if nums[mid] < nums[mid+1]: lo = mid+1; else: hi = mid. Return lo.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We are guaranteed to find a peak because we move towards increasing slope.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: No need to check boundaries as they are -∞.

problems.what_you_learn: Binary search on array with no sort needed.

problems.name: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.description: There is an integer array nums sorted in ascending order (with distinct values). Prior to being passed to your function, nums is possibly rotated at an unknown pivot index. Given the rotated array nums and an integer target, return the index of target if it is in nums, or -1 if it is not. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.
constraints: All values of nums are unique.
nums is guaranteed to be rotated at some pivot.
hints: Use binary search with extra condition to determine which half is sorted.
If left half is sorted (nums[lo] <= nums[mid]), then check if target is in left half; else search right.
Else the right half is sorted; check accordingly.

solution_approach.key_observation: At any mid, one half is sorted. We can use that to decide which side to search.
solution_approach.algorithm: Binary search: while lo <= hi: mid = (lo+hi)//2; if nums[mid] == target return mid. If nums[lo] <= nums[mid]: // left sorted; if target between nums[lo] and nums[mid-1], hi=mid-1; else lo=mid+1. Else: // right sorted; if target between nums[mid+1] and nums[hi], lo=mid+1; else hi=mid-1.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We always search in the correct sorted half.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Careful with equality conditions.

problems.what_you_learn: Binary search in rotated sorted array.

common_mistakes: Using wrong condition to determine sorted half.

problems.description: Given an array of integers nums sorted in non-decreasing order, find the starting and ending position of a given target value. If target is not found in the array, return [-1, -1]. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.

For first: if nums[mid] >= target, hi=mid-1 else lo=mid+1.
For last: if nums[mid] <= target, lo=mid+1 else hi=mid-1.

For first: while lo<=hi: mid; if nums[mid] >= target: hi=mid-1; else lo=mid+1; if lo<n and nums[lo]==target return lo else -1. For last: if nums[mid] <= target: lo=mid+1; else hi=mid-1; if hi>=0 and nums[hi]==target return hi else -1.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We adjust search to find boundaries.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Check bounds carefully.

problems.name: Daily Temperatures
problems.description: Given an array of integers temperatures representing daily temperatures, return an array answer such that answer[i] is the number of days you have to wait after the i-th day to get a warmer temperature. If there is no future day with a warmer temperature, keep answer[i] = 0.

examples.explanation: First day: next warmer is next day (1). Second: next day. Third: wait 4 days for 76. etc.
Each next day is warmer except last.

hints: Use a stack to keep indices of temperatures that haven't found a warmer day.
Iterate through the array; while stack not empty and temperatures[i] > temperatures[stack.top()], pop and set answer[popped] = i - popped.
Push current index onto stack.

solution_approach.key_observation: We need to find next greater element for each index.
solution_approach.algorithm: Use monotonic decreasing stack (indices). For each i, while stack not empty and temps[i] > temps[stack.peek()]: ans[pop] = i - pop. Push i. After loop, remaining have 0.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We maintain indices with decreasing temperatures; when we find a warmer one, we resolve all cooler ones.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Stack holds indices.

problems.what_you_learn: Monotonic stack for next greater element.
common_mistakes: Not updating ans for remaining stack elements.

problems.name: Next Greater Element II
problems.description: Given a circular integer array nums (i.e., the next element of nums[n-1] is nums[0]), return the next greater number for every element in nums. The next greater number of a number x is the first greater number to its traversing-order next in the array, which means you could search circularly to find its next greater number. If it doesn't exist, return -1 for this element.

examples.explanation: For 1: next greater 2; for 2: -1 (wrap around, no greater); for last 1: next greater 2 (wrap).

edge_cases: Strictly increasing (all have next except last, but circular gives -1 for max).
hints: Use a monotonic stack on a doubled array (or process array twice).
Iterate i from 2n-1 down to 0; use stack to find next greater.
Only store results for i < n.

solution_approach.key_observation: We can simulate circular by traversing array twice.
solution_approach.algorithm: Initialize ans with -1. Use stack. For i in range(2*n -1, -1, -1): idx = i % n. While stack and nums[idx] >= nums[stack[-1]]: pop. If stack not empty, ans[idx] = nums[stack[-1]]. Push idx.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We process from right to left, keeping decreasing stack, and wrap around.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Alternatively, loop twice with modulo.

common_mistakes: Not resetting stack for each element.

problems.name: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
problems.description: Evaluate the value of an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation. Valid operators are +, -, *, and /. Each operand may be an integer or another expression. Note that division between two integers should truncate toward zero.

When you encounter an operator, pop two operands, compute, push result.
Order matters for subtraction and division.

solution_approach.why_it_works: Stack maintains operands for the operations.

problems.name: Simplify Path

Return the simplified canonical path.

For '..', pop from stack if not empty.

solution_approach.why_it_works: Stack represents the current directory structure.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Join with '/' and add leading '/'. If stack empty, return '/'.

problems.name: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.description: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. You may return the answer in any order.

solution_approach.why_it_works: Heap maintains the k largest frequencies.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use PriorityQueue with custom comparator.

problems.name: Merge Intervals
problems.description: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i], merge all overlapping intervals, and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals.
hints: Sort intervals by start time.

problems.description: Given an integer array nums of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set). The solution set must not contain duplicate subsets. Return the solution in any order.
hints: Use backtracking: include or exclude each element.
Alternatively, iterate over bit masks.
Common backtracking pattern.

solution_approach.key_observation: Each element can be either included or not.
solution_approach.algorithm: DFS with index: for each index, either include nums[index] or skip. Add current list to result.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Explores all combinations.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use a list to build subset.

common_mistakes: Using extra set to avoid duplicates (but nums unique).

problems.name: Combinations
problems.description: Given two integers n and k, return all possible combinations of k numbers chosen from the range [1, n]. You may return the answer in any order.
hints: Use backtracking: for each start, add number, recurse, backtrack.
Prune: if remaining numbers < k, stop.
Classic combination generation.

solution_approach.key_observation: We choose k numbers from n.
solution_approach.algorithm: DFS with start index. If size == k, add. Else, for i from start to n, add i, recurse with i+1, backtrack.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Explores all combinations without duplicates.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Prune with if n - i + 1 < k - size.

common_mistakes: Not pruning, leading to extra recursion.

problems.name: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
problems.description: Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2 of size m and n respectively, return the median of the two sorted arrays. The overall run time complexity should be O(log (m+n)).
hints: Use binary search on the smaller array to partition.
Ensure left part size equals right part (or +1).
Check max of left <= min of right.

solution_approach.key_observation: We can find the correct partition point.
solution_approach.algorithm: Ensure nums1 is smaller. Binary search on nums1 to find partition. Compute partition2 = (m+n+1)//2 - partition1. Check boundaries. If valid, compute median.
solution_approach.why_it_works: The partition divides the combined array into left and right halves.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Handle edge cases with -inf and inf.

problems.name: Longest Valid Parentheses
problems.description: Given a string containing just the characters '(' and ')', return the length of the longest valid (well-formed) parentheses substring.
hints: Use a stack to track indices of '(' that haven't been matched.
Initialize stack with -1 to handle base.
When encountering ')', pop; if stack empty, push current index; else update max length with i - stack[-1].

solution_approach.key_observation: We can use stack to compute lengths of valid substrings.
solution_approach.algorithm: Stack = [-1]. For i, char: if '(' push i. else: pop; if stack empty push i; else maxLen = max(maxLen, i - stack[-1]).
solution_approach.why_it_works: The stack contains indices of unmatched '(' and the last unmatched ')', allowing length calculation.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Alternative DP.

common_mistakes: Not updating max when stack becomes empty.

problems.name: Trapping Rain Water
problems.description: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining.
hints: Use two pointers: left and right, maintaining left_max and right_max.
If height[left] < height[right], water trapped at left depends on left_max - height[left]; else right.
Move the pointer with smaller height.

solution_approach.key_observation: Water trapped at index i is min(max_left, max_right) - height[i].
solution_approach.algorithm: Two pointers: left=0, right=n-1, left_max=0, right_max=0, ans=0. While left<right: if height[left] < height[right]: update left_max; ans += max(0, left_max - height[left]); left++. Else: update right_max; ans += max(0, right_max - height[right]); right--.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We compute water based on min of max on each side.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: O(1) space.

problems.what_you_learn: Two pointers for trapping rain water.
common_mistakes: Using DP with O(n) space (still fine).

problems.name: Sliding Window Maximum
problems.description: You are given an array of integers nums, there is a sliding window of size k which is moving from the very left of the array to the very right. You can only see the k numbers in the window. Each time the sliding window moves right by one position. Return the max sliding window.
hints: Use a deque (monotonic decreasing) to store indices of potential maximums.
Maintain deque so that elements are in decreasing order of values.
At each step, remove indices out of window, remove smaller elements, add current, and the front is max.

solution_approach.key_observation: We can maintain a monotonic deque of indices with decreasing values.
solution_approach.algorithm: Initialize deque. For i in 0..n-1: while deque and deque[0] < i-k+1: pop front. while deque and nums[deque[-1]] <= nums[i]: pop back. push i. If i >= k-1: add nums[deque[0]] to result.
solution_approach.why_it_works: The deque stores indices of candidates for max in the window.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use List as deque with manual indexing.

problems.what_you_learn: Monotonic deque for sliding window maximum.

problems.name: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
problems.description: Given an array of integers heights representing the histogram's bar height where the width of each bar is 1, return the area of the largest rectangle in the histogram.

examples.explanation: Largest rectangle of height 5 and width 2 (area 10).

hints: Use a monotonic stack to find the nearest smaller element to left and right.
For each bar, the max rectangle with that height spans between smaller bars.
Compute area = heights[i] * (right_smaller - left_smaller - 1).

solution_approach.key_observation: For each bar, we can find the boundaries where it is the minimum.
solution_approach.algorithm: Use stack of indices. Iterate i from 0 to n: while stack and (i==n or heights[i] < heights[stack[-1]]): pop height = heights[stack.pop()]; width = i if stack empty else i - stack[-1] - 1; area = height * width; update max. Push i.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We pop when we find a bar smaller than the top, meaning the popped bar's right boundary is i.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Add a sentinel 0 at end.

problems.what_you_learn: Monotonic stack for largest rectangle in histogram.

problems.name: Minimum Window Substring
problems.description: Given two strings s and t of lengths m and n respectively, return the minimum window substring of s such that every character in t (including duplicates) is included in the window. If there is no such substring, return the empty string.
constraints: s and t consist of uppercase and lowercase English letters.
hints: Use sliding window with two pointers.
Maintain a count of required characters and a counter for matched.
Expand right until all characters are found, then shrink left to minimize.

solution_approach.key_observation: We need to find the smallest window containing all characters of t.
solution_approach.algorithm: Use two pointers left, right. Maintain map of t char counts and a counter for required. Expand right, when all required matched, update min, then shrink left, decrement counts.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We expand to satisfy condition, then contract to find minimum.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use two maps or array of 128.

problems.what_you_learn: Complex sliding window with character counting.
follow_up_concepts: Longest substring with at most k distinct

problems.name: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
problems.description: Design an algorithm to serialize and deserialize a binary tree. Serialization is the process of converting a data structure or object into a sequence of bits so that it can be stored or transmitted. Deserialization is the reverse. You may use any method, but the serialized format must be able to reconstruct the tree.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in range [0, 10^4].

function_signature.dart: String serialize(TreeNode? root); TreeNode? deserialize(String data)

hints: Use BFS or DFS. For BFS, include null markers.
For DFS, use preorder with null markers.
Deserialize by reconstructing using the same order.

solution_approach.key_observation: We can serialize using a delimiter and null marker.
solution_approach.algorithm: Serialization: do BFS or DFS, append node values or 'null' separated by comma. Deserialization: parse tokens and build tree using queue or recursion.
solution_approach.why_it_works: The serialization includes enough info to reconstruct.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use a queue for BFS or index for DFS.

problems.name: Alien Dictionary
problems.description: There is a new alien language which uses the Latin alphabet. However, the order among letters is unknown to you. You receive a list of words from the dictionary, where words are sorted lexicographically by the rules of this new language. Derive the order of letters in this language. If the order is invalid, return an empty string. If there are multiple valid orders, return any of them.
constraints: words[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Build a graph of character order based on adjacent words.
When two words differ at position i, then char1 -> char2.
Perform topological sort (Kahn's algorithm). If cycle, invalid.

solution_approach.key_observation: The ordering is determined by comparing adjacent words.
solution_approach.algorithm: Build graph and indegree. For each adjacent pair, find first differing char, add edge. Then topological sort.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Topological sort gives a valid order if graph is DAG.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Handle prefix case (e.g., 'abc' before 'ab') invalid.

problems.name: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
problems.description: Given an m x n integers matrix, return the length of the longest increasing path in matrix. From each cell, you can move in four directions: left, right, up, or down. You may not move diagonally or move outside the boundary.
hints: Use DFS with memoization: dp[i][j] = longest path starting from (i,j).
Recurrence: dp[i][j] = 1 + max(dp[neighbor]) if matrix[neighbor] > matrix[i][j].
Compute for all cells.

solution_approach.key_observation: Longest increasing path can be computed with DFS and memoization.
solution_approach.algorithm: Define dfs(i,j) returns longest path from (i,j). If memoized, return. Else compute by exploring 4 directions if next value > current, take max+1.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Because we cache results, each cell computed once.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use 2D array for memo.

common_mistakes: Infinite recursion due to cycles (but increasing prevents).

problems.name: Word Search II
problems.description: Given an m x n board of characters and a list of strings words, return all words on the board. Each word must be constructed from letters of sequentially adjacent cells, where adjacent cells are horizontally or vertically neighboring. The same letter cell may not be used more than once in a word.
constraints: board and words consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Use a Trie to store words for efficient prefix matching.
DFS on board, pruning when prefix not in Trie.
Mark visited cells.

solution_approach.key_observation: Trie helps avoid exploring paths that don't lead to any word.
solution_approach.algorithm: Build Trie from words. For each cell, if board[i][j] is in trie children, DFS with node. In DFS, if node is word, add to result. Explore neighbors.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Trie provides pruning.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use a set to avoid duplicates.

problems.what_you_learn: Trie with backtracking for word search.

problems.name: Reconstruct Itinerary
problems.description: You are given a list of airline tickets where tickets[i] = [from_i, to_i] represent the departure and arrival airports. Reconstruct the itinerary in order and return it. All of the tickets belong to a man who departs from 'JFK', so the itinerary must start with 'JFK'. If there are multiple valid itineraries, return the smallest lexicographical order when read as a sequence.
constraints: from_i and to_i consist of uppercase English letters.

Use Hierholzer's algorithm with a stack.
Sort neighbors in lexicographical order to get smallest itinerary.

solution_approach.key_observation: We need to use all edges exactly once.
solution_approach.algorithm: Build graph with adjacency list of destinations sorted in reverse order. Use DFS: while neighbors: pop smallest, recurse; then append airport.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Hierholzer's algorithm gives Eulerian path.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use stack to store result.

common_mistakes: Using recursion that may stack overflow (but E small).

problems.name: Word Ladder
problems.description: Given two words beginWord and endWord, and a dictionary wordList, return the number of words in the shortest transformation sequence from beginWord to endWord, such that only one letter can be changed at a time and each transformed word must exist in wordList. constraints: All words consist of lowercase English letters.

function_signature.generic: ladderLength(beginWord: str, endWord: str, wordList: List[str]) -> int
function_signature.dart: int ladderLength(String beginWord, String endWord, List<String> wordList)

hints: BFS on the graph where words are nodes and edges between words differing by one letter.
Use a set for wordList for O(1) lookup.
For each word, generate all possible one-letter variations.

solution_approach.key_observation: Shortest path in unweighted graph.
solution_approach.algorithm: BFS from beginWord. For each word, generate all possible next words by changing each character to any letter; if in wordList and not visited, add to queue. When endWord found, return steps.
solution_approach.why_it_works: BFS gives shortest path.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use a queue and visited set.

problems.name: Find Median from Data Stream
problems.description: Design a data structure that supports adding integers and finding the median. The median is the middle value in an ordered integer list. If the size is even, the median is the average of the two middle values. Implement the MedianFinder class: addNum(num) adds integer, findMedian() returns double.
constraints: At most 5 * 10^4 calls to addNum and findMedian.

function_signature.dart: class MedianFinder { void addNum(int num); double findMedian(); }

examples.explanation: After adding 1,2 median 1.5; after adding 3 median 2.0.

hints: Use two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half.
Maintain size property: max-heap size is either equal or one more than min-heap.
When adding, add to max-heap, then balance.

solution_approach.key_observation: Heaps can maintain the two halves.
solution_approach.algorithm: maxHeap (lower half, max) and minHeap (upper half, min). Add: if maxHeap empty or num <= maxHeap.peek(): add to max; else min. Balance: if maxHeap.size > minHeap.size+1, move max to min; if minHeap.size > maxHeap.size, move min to max. findMedian: if sizes equal, return (maxHeap.peek()+minHeap.peek())/2.0 else maxHeap.peek().
solution_approach.why_it_works: We keep the largest of lower and smallest of upper.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use PriorityQueue with reversed order for max-heap.

problems.expected_time_complexity: O(log n) per add, O(1) for findMedian

problems.description: You are given an array of k linked-lists, each linked-list is sorted in ascending order. Merge all the linked-lists into one sorted linked-list and return it.

solution_approach.why_it_works: Heap gives the smallest current node.

Careful with edge links.

problems.name: LRU Cache
problems.description: Design a data structure that follows the constraints of a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache. Implement the LRUCache class: LRUCache(capacity) initializes, get(key) returns value or -1, put(key, value) updates or inserts. Both operations should have O(1) average time complexity.
constraints: At most 2 * 10^5 calls to get and put.

function_signature.generic: LRUCache.get(key: int) -> int, put(key: int, value: int) -> None
function_signature.dart: class LRUCache { int get(int key); void put(int key, int value); }

hints: Use a hash map to store key to node in a doubly linked list.
The list maintains order of usage.
Move accessed node to head, and remove tail when evicting.

solution_approach.key_observation: O(1) operations require a map and a list.
solution_approach.algorithm: Use a doubly linked list with dummy head and tail. Map key to node. get: if exists, move to head, return value. put: if exists, update value and move to head; else add new node, if over capacity remove tail.
solution_approach.why_it_works: List gives LRU order, map gives O(1) access.

problems.name: LFU Cache
problems.description: Design and implement a data structure for a Least Frequently Used (LFU) cache. Implement the LFUCache class: LFUCache(capacity) initializes, get(key) returns value or -1, put(key, value) updates or inserts. When the cache reaches its capacity, it should invalidate the least frequently used item. If there is a tie, the least recently used item is evicted.
constraints: At most 2 * 10^5 calls to get and put.

function_signature.generic: LFUCache.get(key: int) -> int, put(key: int, value: int) -> None
function_signature.dart: class LFUCache { int get(int key); void put(int key, int value); }

hints: Maintain a map from frequency to a doubly linked list of keys.
Also maintain a map from key to its node and frequency.
Track min frequency for eviction.

solution_approach.key_observation: We need O(1) operations and frequency-based eviction.
solution_approach.algorithm: Use keyNode map, freqMap map from freq to LinkedHashSet of keys. get: increment frequency and move key to new freq set. put: if key exists, update; else if capacity full, evict from minFreq set. Add new key with freq 1.
solution_approach.why_it_works: Freq sets maintain LRU within same frequency.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use LinkedHashSet or custom doubly linked list.

common_mistakes: Not maintaining LRU order within same frequency.

problems.name: Edit Distance
problems.description: Given two strings word1 and word2, return the minimum number of operations required to convert word1 to word2. You have the following three operations permitted: Insert a character, Delete a character, Replace a character.
constraints: word1 and word2 consist of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: horse -> rorse (replace h->r) -> rose (remove r) -> ros (remove e).

hints: Use DP table dp[i][j] = minimum edits for word1[0..i-1] and word2[0..j-1].
Recurrence: if chars equal, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]; else min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]) + 1.
Base cases: dp[i][0]=i, dp[0][j]=j.

solution_approach.key_observation: Optimal substructure: edit distance can be built from smaller prefixes.
solution_approach.algorithm: Build dp table of size (m+1)x(n+1). Initialize first row and column. Fill using recurrence. Return dp[m][n].
solution_approach.why_it_works: DP covers all edit operations.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Can optimize space to O(n).

problems.name: Regular Expression Matching
problems.description: Given an input string s and a pattern p, implement regular expression matching with support for '.' and '*' where '.' matches any single character, and '*' matches zero or more of the preceding element. The matching should cover the entire input string (not partial).
constraints: p contains lowercase English letters, '.', '*', and '*' can only follow a character.
hints: Use DP with dp[i][j] meaning s[0..i-1] matches p[0..j-1].
If p[j-1] == '*', consider zero or more of preceding character.
Recurrence: if p[j-1] != '*', then dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] if match. Else: dp[i][j] = dp[i][j-2] (zero) or (match and dp[i-1][j]).

solution_approach.key_observation: DP handles the '*' repetitions.
solution_approach.algorithm: Create dp table. Initialize dp[0][0]=true. For j, if p[j-1]=='*', dp[0][j]=dp[0][j-2]. Then fill: if match, dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1]; if '*', dp[i][j] = dp[i][j-2] or (match and dp[i-1][j]).
solution_approach.why_it_works: DP covers all matching options.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Use 0-indexing for strings.

problems.name: First Missing Positive
problems.description: Given an unsorted integer array nums, return the smallest missing positive integer. Your algorithm should run in O(n) time and use O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: Place each number in its correct position: nums[i] should be at index nums[i]-1.
Swap until correct.
Then find first index where nums[i] != i+1.

solution_approach.key_observation: We can use the array itself as a hash map.
solution_approach.algorithm: For i in 0..n-1: while nums[i] in [1..n] and nums[i] != nums[nums[i]-1]: swap. After that, iterate and return first i where nums[i] != i+1.
solution_approach.why_it_works: We put numbers in their correct positions.
solution_approach.implementation_notes: Handle out-of-range numbers.

problems.what_you_learn: In-place array hashing for missing positive.
common_mistakes: Infinite loop if swap condition wrong.
